finding.claim: POST /restore passes an unauthenticated, unsigned request parameter directly to Marshal.load, which can instantiate arbitrary Ruby objects and enables deserialization-based remote code execution, depending on gadget classes loaded in the process.
finding.source: params[:state] from the POST body or query string of POST /restore (app.rb:5-6); attacker-controlled with no precondition.

trace.note: Route post "/restore" accepts any request; no before-filter or auth check in the file.
Base64.decode64 is lenient; it only decodes the attacker's encoding to raw bytes.
Marshal.load parses bytes into live Ruby objects and runs deserialization hooks on any class available in the process.
state.inspect is returned to the caller, giving the attacker feedback (not required for exploitation).

finding.guards_checked: No authentication/authorization in app.rb; no HMAC, signature, or encryption on the state blob; no class allowlist or safe loader; Base64 is encoding, not a control; no size or content-type limits. Expertise case 18 (unsafe deserializer on untrusted content) applies. Gadget availability not verified (gem lock not inspected, endpoint not run).

verdict.reason: app.rb:5 declares an unauthenticated `post "/restore"` route, and app.rb:6 passes `Base64.decode64(params[:state])` straight into `Marshal.load` with no signature, HMAC, class allowlist, or size limit, so an anonymous attacker controls the bytes deserialized; app.rb:7 returns `state.inspect`, which only adds feedback. The directory contains only app.rb (no Gemfile or lock file), so whether a usable gadget chain exists in the running process is unverified. The candidate's claim is hedged on that point, so the vulnerable sink itself stands.
